newsitem.title: RWANDA: Zaire fighting intensifies, U.N. prepares pullout.
newsitem.headline: Zaire fighting intensifies, U.N. prepares pullout.

text.p: Fighting between Zairean troops and Tutsi rebels raged near the eastern city of Goma on Thursday and aid agencies responsible for feeding more than a million Hutu refugees prepared to evacuate, aid officials said.
Incoming and outgoing mortar bombs and heavy weapons fire centered on an area about two km (one mile) north of Goma during the day, but by nightfall the firing was sporadic.
Reuters correspondent Buchizya Mseteka travelled with rebels inside Zaire and reported a swathe of territory from Lake Tanganyika to Lake Kivu was in rebel hands after a lightning campaign.
The rebellion is seen as the biggest challenge yet for President Mobutu Sese Seko, one of Africa's longest-surviving dictators but now ailing with cancer in Switzerland.
In the town of Uvira, captured by rebels a week ago, rebel leader Laurent Kabila told thousands of cheering people: "We must remove Mobutu and throw him into the dustbin of history."
Kabila, a stout 56-year-old veteran of a rebellion crushed by Mobutu's forces in the 1960s, told the crowds: "This is your movement. It is a movement against tyranny and corruption."
The fiercest fighting on Thursday was near Goma, just across the border from the Rwandan town of Gisenyi and centre for international efforts to feed 1.1 million Rwandan Hutu refugees.
"Aid agencies have been told to prepare for a 70 to 100 percent evacuation from Goma," said Steve Pratt of CARE International by telephone from Goma.
"This would take place by road to the south to Rwanda. We have been told to stay put in our houses until the decision is taken," said Pratt.
But other aid workers said even an evacuation by road would be hard as more than 50 aid agency vehicles had been seized, most of them by Zairean soldiers, in the last 48 hours in Goma.

"Goma is in the process of falling as I talk to you. Government forces are running away. There is a big battle going on in Goma and within two days we will have full control of the city," Kabila said at Uvira.
"Goma airport is under the control of our military forces."
But a U.N. official said journalists were taken to the airport on Thursday afternoon and it was still in Zairean army hands.
Bloated corpses floating down the river marking Zaire's border suggest the scale of the slaughter in the past two weeks.

At least 13 corpses, including the body of a young child lay in the sun on Thursday on the banks of Lake Tanganyika on the Burundian side of the border with eastern Zaire. Fishermen said they had buried about 50 in total.
"There are lots and lots of corpses which have come down here. Most of them we just buried as they smelled so bad. There were perhaps 50 in all," one fisherman told Reuters.

In the Zaire town of Bukavu, scene of savage fighting for days, priests said on Thursday that it was still too dangerous to bury the body of Roman Catholic Archbishop Christophe Munzihirwa killed in a military attack there two days ago.
"They said that they could not do the funeral because it was not possible to take the body to the cathedral," one priest in contact with Bukavu said.
International attention has focused largely on the plight of the 1.1 million Hutu refugees in Zaire. Hutus massacred nearly one million Tutsis in Rwanda in 1994 and then fled en masse to Zaire.
The contagion from the 1994 genocide spread to Zaire and lies at the root of today's conflict.

U.N. refugee agency official Panos Moumtzis said leaders in Kahindo camp north of Goma with some 110,000 residents decided on Wednesday to move towards Mugunga camp, to the west of the city, and had done so at first light.
"They are now taking a path through the mountains," he said. He added they were accompanied by about 20,000 Zaireans.
Mugunga, with a population of about 400,000, is already the world's biggest, most densely packed refugee camp.
"Mugunga is becoming a magnet, everyone heads there thinking it is a safe haven," said Michelle Quintaglie of the World Food Programme. "Even Zaireans living near the airport are coming down."
She said against all odds some local staff from CARE and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies managed to distribute some food in Mugunga on Thursday.

Paul Stromberg, a UNHCR (U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees) spokesman in the Rwandan capital Kigali, said on Thursday he believed the Tutsi rebels were deliberating striking at all aid routes to cut supplies to the refugees.

"It seems to be their strategy to cut supply lines for the refugees. The roads (to Goma) have been impassable since October 20 and yesterday the World Food Programme announced they would fly food into Goma today. And today the airport is attacked," he said. "It appears not to be a mere coincidence."
